items.title: Trump voters are not pumped about voting in the midterms, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
Oct 8 (Reuters) - Voters who backed Democratic former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 are far more enthusiastic about casting ballots this November than ​those who supported President Donald Trump, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found, in a potential warning sign for Republicans heading into the midterm elections.

The six-day poll, completed Monday, also found that men were more enthusiastic ‌about voting and more certain to cast ballots than women, and that male voters showed signs of shifting toward Democrats. That could signal erosion in Republican support among a demographic that was a pillar of Trump's 2024 victory.

Some 48% of 2024 Harris voters said they were "very enthusiastic" about voting in the November 3 midterm elections, when control of both chambers of Congress is at stake. By comparison, just 30% of Trump voters said the same in the poll.

The findings add ​to evidence of an enthusiasm gap favoring Democrats and suggest potential cracks in the coalition that propelled Trump in 2024, when he won the popular vote. That coalition was fueled by ​strong support from men and gains among Hispanic voters and other demographic groups that shifted to the right in the 2024 election.

The poll also adds to ⁠a string of encouraging signs for Democrats, who are widely favored to win control of the House of Representatives and remain competitive in the fight for the Senate as Trump's approval ratings have ​slipped amid voter concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.

Republican strategist Charlie Gerow said the poll's findings raise the stakes for his party's turnout efforts, though he expects the enthusiasm gap ​to narrow as concerns about what he described as far-left Democrats gaining power motivate Republican voters.

"The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what's going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections," Gerow said.

While Trump voters overwhelmingly plan to vote Republican and Harris voters are similarly inclined to vote Democratic, the president's 2024 supporters are less decided, with 13% saying they aren't sure who to vote for in congressional elections, compared to 7% of ​Harris supporters who say the same.

The poll, which was conducted nationwide and surveyed 4,506 adults online, showed that just 32% of Americans approved of Trump's presidency, holding at a record ​low first marked in a September Reuters/Ipsos survey. The survey has a 2 percentage point margin of error.

Since taking office in January 2025, support for Trump has fallen across every major demographic group, including double-digit drops among Hispanics, ‌men, rural ⁠and suburban voters, people without college degrees and evangelical Christians.

One notable shift has come among men, a group Trump won in all three of his presidential campaigns, including by a 12-point margin in 2024, according to a Pew Research analysis.

When asked how they would vote in a congressional race if the elections were today, men in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll picked Democrats over Republicans, 43% to 39%. The four-point Democratic advantage was the widest of Trump's second term. Men consistently favored Republicans in 2025 but since August have mostly favored Democrats.

The warning signs for Republicans reflect growing voter concerns about the high cost of living amid a ​surge in gasoline and diesel prices following the ​war with Iran. Trump launched the Iran attacks in ⁠February, despite pledging during his campaign not to start new conflicts and to lower costs for consumers.

Cost of living is the top issue on Americans' minds as they decide how they will vote next month, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Voters cite democratic values as the second biggest issue, followed by immigration.

Republicans ​continue to hold an edge among older voters, a crucial bloc in midterm elections, when seniors have historically accounted for an outsized share of ​the electorate. Voters 50 and ⁠older still favor the Republican Party over the Democratic Party by 2 percentage points, 44% to 42%, though that was down from an 8-point Republican advantage in December.

Still, the enthusiasm gap looms large for Republicans.

Among all the voters in the poll who said they were enthusiastic, 62% said they were pumped about expressing opposition to Trump, compared to 36% who said they were eager to support the president.

Linda Rivera, a 46-year-old Trump voter in ⁠Pennsylvania, said that ​while she would probably vote Republican if she casts a ballot, she is frustrated with both parties and feels “neither enthusiastic ​or unenthusiastic” about voting next month.

Rivera, a respondent in the poll, said concerns about widespread voting fraud - which have been repeatedly fanned by Trump and his Republican allies without evidence - have added to her doubts about whether she will vote.

"I have lost ​faith in the voting process," she told Reuters. "I have lost faith in both parties. Not just one."

items.title: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
items.content_html:
Oct 7 (Reuters) - The interest rate on the most common US home loan jumped last ‌week to its highest in almost three years, worsening affordability for buyers four weeks before elections that will decide if President Donald Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress.

The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage surged 19 basis points to 7.49% in the week ended October 2, the Mortgage ​Bankers Association said on Wednesday. It was last higher in November 2023.

Mortgage rates are tied closely to ​the yield on US 10-year Treasury notes, which earlier this week hit a 24-year high, driven ⁠by worries over inflationary pressures from soaring oil prices and data showing stronger US economic growth.

The cost of ​living is the top issue on Americans' minds as they decide how they will vote on November 3, a ​Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday showed, and is one reason why Trump's approval rating is at a record low of 32%.

Home borrowing rates are up about 1.4 percentage points since joint US-Israeli strikes against Iran began in late February, tracking a similar rise in the 10-year ​Treasury yield, which topped 5.3% on Monday.

Inflation is also on the rise, registering 3.4% in August by a measure ​that the Federal Reserve targets at 2%.

Fed policymakers have signaled they expect to follow their September interest-rate increase with another rate ‌hike by ⁠year's end, though markets are for now betting they will not move at their upcoming policy meeting at the end of October.

Asked by a reporter Wednesday about mortgage rates, Trump called Fed chairman Kevin Warsh "great," but added the rest of the board "would like to see the country do badly, in my opinion, because I think interest rates ​should come down."

US Treasury ​Secretary Scott Bessent, in ⁠the Oval Office with Trump, blamed inflation and high mortgage rates on the temporary shock from higher oil prices. "So once we get on the other side of this Iran ​conflict, (the) energy market is going to be well supplied, and we will move down ​towards the Fed's ⁠target and mortgage rates and the 10-year will come back down," Bessent said.

Mortgage loan applications fell 4.2% last week from the previous week, the MBA said on Wednesday, with refinancing applications dropping sharply. Overall application volumes are the lowest since February ⁠2025 ​and have fallen nearly 50% since January.

"Very few homeowners have an incentive ​to refinance at these rates, and the jump in borrowing costs has caused many potential borrowers to step back from the purchase market," ​said Joel Kan, the MBA’s deputy chief economist.

items.title: Most Republicans in tight midterm races distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds
items.content_html:
Oct 7 (Reuters) - Two-thirds of Republican candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with President Donald Trump on policy or played down ties to him, a Reuters review found, revealing a widespread effort to distance themselves from the president as his unpopularity threatens the party's hold on Congress.

The review ​of voting records, public statements and campaign materials found candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races seeking some distance from Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

The candidates have largely criticized or ‌diverged from Trump on individual issues rather than repudiated his broader agenda. The findings suggest an effort to attract independent voters while avoiding a direct break with their party leader.

Policy differences were the most common point of divergence, appearing in 23 of the 62 races.

In 12 contests, the split centered on the Iran conflict, with vulnerable Republicans either voting to curb Trump's war powers or calling publicly for an end to the fighting that has raised gas prices and squeezed household budgets.

Data centers are among the issues dividing Trump and some Republican candidates. ​Reuters identified three candidates in competitive races who have criticized or sought to slow such projects despite the president's support for faster development.

The shift is notable because Trump has spent the past decade remaking the Republican ​Party in his own image and has been swift to punish lawmakers and candidates who defied him through primary challenges, personal attacks or public pressure to fall into line.

In response ⁠to questions about the Reuters findings, White House spokesman Davis Ingle pointed to the administration's accomplishments and said Trump was "the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator" for the party.

While news organizations have highlighted individual cases of distancing, the ​Reuters review is the first to systematically measure the trend across competitive races that will decide whether Republicans retain control of either or both chambers of Congress.

A new Reuters/Ipsos poll underscored the challenge facing Republicans: Trump's approval rating remained stuck at a ​career-low 32%, while registered voters favored Democrats over Republicans 44% to 37% ahead of the midterms. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%.

Reuters also found a broad effort to play down ties: A dozen candidates removed his name, image or endorsements from campaign websites, most after securing their party's nomination.

Others acted in subtler ways, skipping his events or declining to say whether he should campaign on their behalf.

Direct criticism was relatively rare, underscoring Trump's dominance of the Republican Party and the risks candidates face in openly challenging a president ​who still commands the loyalty of many ardent supporters.

Candidates distancing themselves from an unpopular president before an election is not unusual. Democrats employed similar tactics in the 2014 and 2022 elections.

While Reuters did not conduct a comparable review of competitive ​races in the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term, analysts said Trump has rarely faced such widespread pushback by vulnerable Republican candidates.

"(Candidates) are reflecting voter attitudes in these races," said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean. "If (voters) are not with Trump, then they need to show ‌a break."

Privately, campaign ⁠advisers told Reuters that candidates needed to dial back ties to Trump to attract independent voters. Publicly, they dismissed criticism of the repositioning.

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, who faces a tough challenge from independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, exemplifies the 11 candidates identified by Reuters who broke with Trump on one policy issue while backing him on everything else.

The balancing act was on display this week when Ricketts, who criticized Trump's plan to expand beef imports, joined the president at a Nebraska rally.

"President Trump, I have been fighting for you in Washington," Ricketts told the crowd.

Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican in one of the country's most competitive House races in Iowa, has also shown a growing willingness to break with the administration. She was ​among 12 candidates identified by Reuters who split with Trump ​on multiple issues, criticizing his beef-import policy and later ⁠voting to limit his war powers in Iran after previously opposing similar measures.

Yet, less than two weeks after her war-powers vote, Miller-Meeks joined Trump at the White House to announce a major steel plant investment in Iowa.

"It is a balancing act," said Republican consultant Jeanette Hoffman, adding that candidates are trying to capitalize on the administration’s successes while creating some ​distance from Trump because of “how toxic the Trump brand is at the moment.”

As Republicans in competitive races seek to expand their appeal beyond Trump's core supporters, ​some candidates have begun dialing back ⁠public displays of loyalty to the president.

Mike Beltran, a former Florida state representative running against Democratic US Representative Kathy Castor, is among candidates who have scrubbed prominent references to Trump from their campaign websites.

In August, his homepage featured a photo of Trump and said he stood with the president, according to the Wayback Machine, an internet archive website. Now Beltran's homepage shows only him and his family and makes no mention of Trump.

Beltran's campaign had no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment.

Representative Mike Lawler ⁠of New York, ​facing one of the most competitive US House races, embodies the balancing act confronting many Republicans in battleground districts: staying close to Trump while ​demonstrating independence from him.

Lawler has highlighted breaks with Trump on issues including temporary legal protections for Haitian immigrants and a Trump-backed proposal to restore Turkey's access to F-35 fighter jets.

His campaign manager Ciro Riccardi said Lawler acts on behalf of his constituency regardless of a president's stance.

Lawler acknowledged the ​disagreements in a speech to Trump supporters at the Republican midterm convention in September, saying, "The truth is that the president and I don't always agree. And that's OK."

items.title: Trump rallies for Paxton in third Texas trip in a month as Republicans defend stronghold
items.content_html:
SAN ANTONIO, Texas, Oct 7 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in a month on Wednesday to campaign for Republicans who now face unexpectedly tight midterm election battles as the ​party seeks to retain control of Congress.

Trump appeared on stage in a packed San Antonio arena with Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a close race with Democrat James Talarico. A loss ‌on November 3 would complicate the party's path to retaining its slim Senate majority and mark a major setback in a Republican stronghold.

Trump expressed appreciation for Paxton's loyalty. He endorsed Paxton in the primary after faulting the incumbent Republican senator, John Cornyn, for not supporting him during tough times.

"He was with us all the way," Trump said of Paxton. "He's a fantastic man and what a job he's done."

Paxton, called up on stage by Trump, thanked the president.

"Mr. President I want to thank you for coming for ​me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas. We are going to win this race," he said.

Supporters, some waving cowboy hats, cheered for Trump and shouted "USA," drowning out several protesters who ​interrupted the event multiple times in a Texas city led by a Democrat. Trump said the protesters should "get the hell out of here."

The rally was Trump's latest ⁠effort to mobilize his supporters for Paxton after staging an unusual mi dterm conventionin Dallas, in part to boost Paxton's campaign. But Trump has also publicly criticized his longtime ally, calling Paxton "a pain in the ass sometimes" last week ​before adding that Republicans "need Ken so badly."

Trump's repeated trips to Texas are part of a broader push in Republican-leaning states, which were expected to be safely in hand but have instead become midterm battlegrounds. His 32-day campaign blitz ​has taken him through Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, while Vice President JD Vance has campaigned in Alaska. Trump and Vance carried all six states in the 2024 presidential election.

Republicans are struggling as voters focus on high costs and the war with Iran, giving Trump record-low approval ratings. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday put his approval at 32%, with Democrats leading Republicans 44% to 37% among registered voters.

Trump on Wednesday repeated comments he had made during a rally in Nebraska on Monday suggesting that Iran ​could attack Los Angeles or San Diego. Trump portrayed such rhetoric, which had drawn criticism from California's Democratic leaders and some Republicans, as underlining the stakes of the war he started on Iran.

Trump surprised some Republicans in ​May by backing Paxton in a party runoff over Cornyn, whom party leaders saw as a safer bet. Republicans are now spending heavily to defend territory they once expected to win comfortably.

Trump won the state by 14 points in 2024, ‌but recent polls ⁠have shown Talarico ahead of Paxton. Republicans are also defending competitive House of Representatives seats in South Texas. Both Trump and Paxton attacked Talarico repeatedly in their remarks.

For Trump, the stakes are also personal. James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, said losing the Senate race would be "devastating for Republicans and devastating for Donald Trump" given his support for Paxton. "I think the president clearly will do a lot to try to avoid that outcome," Henson said.

Trump's political operation has also poured millions into competitive House races. In San Antonio, Republican Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran, is running in a newly redrawn district, part ​of a Republican-led remapping that Democrats have called a ​partisan gerrymander. De La Cruz is expected to ⁠speak at Wednesday's rally.

Trump relationship with Paxton has appeared awkward at times. Paxton was recorded telling donors that Republican candidates' numbers fell after the Trump-centered convention in Dallas, according to the New York Times, while Trump has publicly mocked Paxton's manner of speaking, clothes and appearance.

"So to be honest with you, the numbers, when we did that convention, ​it dropped our numbers. Everybody's numbers dropped," Paxton said in the recording. His campaign has disputed suggestions that the remarks amounted to criticism of Trump. A ​spokesperson did not respond to a ⁠request for comment.

A New York Times/Siena College poll released October 3 showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said rallying Trump's base was "necessary but not sufficient" for Paxton.

"Trump's visits are a catch-22," Rottinghaus said. "The president can inspire as much as he can repel."

Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is also in a closer-than-expected re-election race, planned to skip Wednesday's rally, citing other campaign events.

"My rallies ⁠are saving the ​Republican Party, again," Trump said in an all-caps post on Truth Social on Tuesday.

Republicans are betting Trump can still turn out the ​voters who powered his 2024 victory even as his broader standing has weakened.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that just 24% of Hispanic voters approved of his performance. They were an important part of Trump's success in 2024, when he won nearly half the Hispanic vote, ​and are a bigger demographic in Texas than most states.

items.title: Trump threatens to fire political advisers if their interests conflict
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - President Donald Trumpsaid on Wednesday he would fire ‌two top election advisers if their work for a Bosnian territorial government posed a conflict of interest weeks ahead of critical US elections, then concluded that it did not.

The two advisers, Chris LaCivita and James Blair, traveled to the self-governing territory ​of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina ahead of elections there on Sunday, according to a New York ​Times report on Tuesday. The newspaper said Republika Srpska's government retained and paid ⁠them to advise on voting issues.

Trump was caught off guard by the Republican duo's trip at a ​critical time in US domestic politics and was angered, a Trump ally familiar with internal White House dynamics said ​on Wednesday.

"Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. "I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate ​them, immediately!"

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office later, Trump said, "They don't have a conflict."

The statement signaled ​a potential rift between a Republican president fighting to maintain slim congressional majorities in the November 3 midterm elections and the ‌pair ⁠of advisers he had charged with leading outside campaign operations.

LaCivita and Blair did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the president's post. The White House also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The United States, Russia and the European Union have been vying for influence over Bosnia.

In April, ​Trump called Blair "one of ​the brightest political minds ⁠in the Country" in a social media post as he stepped away from his role as White House deputy chief of staff. At the time, the president said ​Blair would work "to prepare Republicans to DEFY LONGSTANDING HISTORY AND WIN the Midterms."

Since ​then, he ⁠has overseen Trump's outside political funding arm, MAGA Inc., that has raked in hundreds of millions of dollars to boost Republican candidates nationwide.

But even with a Republican cash advantage over Democrats, the map of competitive US Senate ⁠and ​US House races continues to expand, threatening Republican majorities in ​both chambers.

LaCivita, a Marine veteran, is a well-known Republican strategist who helped lead Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.

items.title: Rubio, in Athens, ties ancient values to 'America First'
items.content_html:
ATHENS, Oct 7 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday urged Western nations to embrace the ancient Greek values of "heroism, honor, and duty", tying the ideals to President Donald Trump's "America First" agenda.

"It's become ​fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the global ​community over one's own people," Rubio told Greek officials, diplomats ⁠and other invitees.

With the ruins of the Parthenon in the distance behind him, ​he said the men of ancient Greece "knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong ​about loyalty to your nation."

Rubio, a potential contender for the Republican nomination to succeed Trump in 2028, delivered the speech from the Pnyx, where ancient Athens' popular assembly once met.

Rubio's speech ​echoed Vice President JD Vance's February 2025 Munich Security Conference speech, which cast Europe's ​challenges as a retreat from shared Western values and drew rebukes from the continent's leaders.

That was ‌followed ⁠by Trump's November 2025 National Security Strategy, which warned that Europe faced "civilization erasure" from migration and challenges to national sovereignty.

"Today, we find ourselves at a crossroads, because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century," ​Rubio said. "The course ​we take will ⁠determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of ​atrophy, and servitude, and decline."

"Under President Trump, the United States has made ​its choice," ⁠Rubio added. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power."

Rubio is visiting three European NATO allies as part of a trip that began in Iceland. Earlier on Wednesday, Rubio and his Greek counterpart ⁠reaffirmed ​close US-Greek security, energy and trade ties. He ​concludes the trip with talks with Portuguese officials on Thursday in Lisbon.

items.title: Florida asks court to force Meta to change Facebook, Instagram for teens
items.content_html:
Oct 7 (Reuters) - Florida ​asked a state judge on Wednesday to order changes to Instagram and Facebook to better ‌protect young users, pressing ahead with a lawsuit accusing parent Meta Platforms (META.O), opens new tab of harming teens after most states resolved similar claims through a sweeping settlement.

In a filing in a Pasco County court, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier asked for a temporary injunction ​forcing Meta to identify and remove users in the state under the age of 14 from ​those platforms, limit teens there to two hours a day across all apps and ⁠turn off features like autoplay and infinite scroll for them.

The filing asked that the changes be implemented immediately ​and be in place while the lawsuit moves forward.

A Meta spokesperson in a statement said after the company's ​settlement with nearly every other state, Florida should focus on getting other platforms to take action.

"The attorney general should be using taxpayer resources to get YouTube and TikTok to empower parents and protect teens in Florida. We regret that he has chosen ​instead to pursue a meritless preliminary injunction years into the litigation," the spokesperson said.

Florida's lawsuit against Meta, which ​accuses the company of knowingly engineering its platforms to be addictive for young users and misleading consumers about its safety, was ‌one ⁠of dozens of similar lawsuits filed by states across the country.

In August, Meta reached settlements with 48 of the other states and Washington, DC, agreeing to pay up to $18 billion and make changes for teen users of its platforms.

Meta has said it works hard to keep teens safe on its platforms, and the company denied wrongdoing ​in agreeing to settle. The ​total payout represents about ⁠three to four months of profit and about one month of revenue for Meta.

Uthmeier, a Republican, opted not to join the settlement and proceed with his lawsuit.

Florida said ​in the filing that the settlement amounted to a “mere slap on the wrist, ​will be cynically ⁠viewed as the cost of doing business, and in any event will not prevent this kind of behavior going forward.”

The changes Uthmeier's filing seeks are more stringent than those the company agreed to as part of that settlement, ⁠as they ​would cut off teens' access to messaging after their time ​limits are hit and bar the company from showing them advertisements.

The changes Meta agreed to make as part of the settlement are an ​indication these changes are possible, Uthmeier's office argued.

items.title: Californians blast Trump remark that Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles, San Diego
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Oct 6 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump suggested to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska that ​Iran could "take out" a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing a swift rebuke from California's Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans.

Trump, speaking at a political ‌rally in the state's farm belt on Monday, discussed American wartime economic sacrifices and said he was determined to "see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did."

"And again, remember, with the war, it's just artificial, it's a little bit high, it's a small price to pay," he told the crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, apparently referring to rising prices of fuel, fertilizer and other products attributed to energy market disruptions from the war.

"It's a small price to ​pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego. This is a ​very small price to pay, and it's going to be over with very soon," he said.

"It's essentially almost over with," Trump went on. "But it's going to ⁠end very soon, and it's going to end one way or the other."

On Tuesday, the White House dismissed criticism of the remark. "The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. ​He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung said in a social media post. "America is safer because of ​the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money."

Trump has shrugged off cost-of-living concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before, and he previously downplayed his concerns about the potential for Iran or its allies to launch an attack on US soil.

The comment in rural Nebraska, a state Trump won with more than 55% of the vote in the 2024 presidential election, targeted Democratic-run cities in California, a solidly Democratic ​state the president often criticizes.

Monday's comments prompted a backlash from California officials.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, denounced the Republican president as "deranged and dangerous."

"After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald ​Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego," he wrote on X.

Newsom, who has positioned himself as a major political foil to Trump and is seen as a potential 2028 presidential ‌candidate, juxtaposed a ⁠video clip of Trump in Nebraska with mention of the president's previous rhetoric to justify deploying US military troops to Los Angeles and other cities to fight crime and enforce immigration.

California's early voting for the November midterm elections started on Monday. The president's Republican Party has hoped to win more races in the state in recent years, including this year's gubernatorial election.

Newsom championed the redrawing of California's congressional map last year to favor Democrats in this year's election after Trump pushed for conservative-led Texas to redraw its map to boost Republicans.

One of the Republicans running in a competitive race in a redrawn California district near ​San Diego, Jim Desmond, distanced himself from Trump's remarks.

"I ​vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America ⁠must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland," he wrote on X. "No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage."

US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent ​who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in a competitive race in northern California, said in a statement that Trump's comment was "unhelpful."

Los ​Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a ⁠Democrat, said in a statement that Trump's comment "could potentially compromise our safety."

Appearing on MS Now on Tuesday, Bass disputed Cheung's assertion that Trump's comments were being misinterpreted by a "freaked out" media.

"Well, I'm not sure that he understands that we can hear what the president said," Bass countered, adding that Cheung's defense of Trump's remarks "has no connection to the words that came out of the president's mouth."

Los Angeles and San Diego rank as the ⁠largest and ​second-largest cities in California by population.

More than 115,000 active-duty service members are also stationed in San Diego, including Naval Base ​San Diego, the largest on the US west coast.

"My constituents — including many active duty service members, veterans, and their families — are not acceptable collateral damage in Trump’s stupid war," US Representative Sara Jacobs, a Democrat, said in a social media post.

(This story has been refiled to fix the dateline to Oct 6, not Oct 5.)

items.title: Trump approval at record low; Hispanic voters sour on Republicans, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 5 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's approval rating held at a record ‌low in recent days, as many Hispanic voters panned his job performance and planned to spurn his Republican Party in next month's midterm elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.

The six-day poll showed 32% of Americans giving a thumbs up to Trump's presidency, unchanged from ​a September Reuters/Ipsos survey that saw the leader's rating at the lowest of his political career.

Hispanic voters helped ​propel Trump to victory in the 2024 presidential contest, when he won nearly half the ⁠Hispanic vote compared with roughly one-third in the 2020 election. But support for the president has waned in recent ​months as Americans struggle with high inflation triggered by Trump's decision to go to war with Iran.

Just 24% of Hispanic Americans ​approve of Trump's performance in the White House, the lowest share in either of Trump's two presidential terms.

The poll gave numerous signs that Trump's low popularity was weighing heavily on his Republican Party, with registered voters preferring Democrats over Republicans by 44% to ​37% less than a month before the November 3 election. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% ​of independent registered voters still undecided.

Just 26% of Hispanic registered voters plan to vote Republican in the contest, which will determine control of ‌both ⁠chambers of Congress during the last two years of Trump's current term. Some 52% of Hispanic voters plan to vote for Democrats, about double the level of support for Republicans and the largest Democratic advantage since Trump took office.

Republicans are bracing for a rough performance in the congressional elections. Many analysts have predicted Democrats will take a majority in the House ​of Representatives, with control of ​the Senate also increasingly ⁠seen as up for grabs.

Cost of living is the top issue on Americans' minds as they decide how they will vote next month, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Consumer inflation has ​spiked following a surge in gasoline and diesel prices brought on by the war with ​Iran that Trump ⁠launched in February.

Republicans' advantage among older Americans has dwindled this year. Voters age 50 or older preferred Trump's party over the Democratic Party by just 2 percentage points — 44% to 42% — compared to an 8-point Republican advantage in December.

The 50-and-older demographic is particularly ⁠important for ​midterm elections when older Americans historically have made up large shares of ​the electorate. Among voters under age 50, Democrats led by 18 points.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, surveyed 4,506 US adults and ​had a margin of error of about two percentage points.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US consumer watchdog examiners adopt lighter touch amid pressure and threats, sources say
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Examiners at the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau gave a largely clean bill of health to most of the companies they inspected earlier this year, a light-touch approach that marked a departure ​from the past for the watchdog, according to three people with knowledge of the matter.

The CFPB resumed examinations in the spring after President Donald Trump's administration had suspended most of the ‌agency's work upon taking office last year.

More than half of those exams went through an "expedited review," which means supervisors identified at most only minor lapses with little risk of harm to consumers, making penalties unlikely, the people said.

Such reviews are more lenient and were historically rare, said the people. But the agency's new political leadership had made it clear via policy changes and other communications that thorough scrutiny was unwelcome and that examiners' jobs were at risk, they added.

The high proportion of expedited reviews, which Reuters is reporting for the first ​time, could expose consumers to harm if the agency overlooked or minimized serious problems, supervisory experts and former agency officials said.

It also shows how the administration's effort to cut federal workers, narrow exams, and encourage companies ​to report officials they feel are too tough on them is reshaping frontline oversight of the financial industry, they added.

Representatives for the CFPB did not respond to requests ⁠for comment. The White House referred Reuters to the CFPB.

The Trump administration says financial industry oversight has become too onerous, hurting lending and the broader economy, though consumer advocates dispute that. It has also said ​it is trying to focus examiners on core risks.

Russell Vought, the CFPB's former acting director, has accused the agency's staff of "thuggery" in their dealings with firms. He told lawmakers in July that it has shifted its supervisory approach with ​the aim of doing "as little damage as possible," adding: "That doesn't mean we're taking an approach to do... as little as possible."

After initially vowing to abolish the CFPB — which Congress created in the wake of the 2007-2009 global financial crisis — the administration tried to slash two thirds of its workforce, including the vast majority of supervisory staff.

Those plans are now on pause pending confirmation of a new CFPB director.

The agency last year said it would cut the number of exams by half and refocus them away from what had been core areas, ​such as student loans and medical debt, and more toward mortgages and redress for military service members. It also said it would mostly focus exams on banks rather than nonbanks, such as payday lenders, which the CFPB ​alone oversees at the federal level.

The agency also now requires examiners to recite a "humility pledge" during exams to work efficiently, transparently and collaboratively with the company concerned. Reuters reported in August that a top CFPB examiner reminded staff of that pledge and warned of "most ‌unpleasant" consequences if ⁠they were too aggressive.

Larry Lee, a former CFPB attorney who left the agency in August, said examiners have no incentive to look diligently for violations in the current climate, even as companies benefit long term from robust oversight.

"Today's undiscovered compliance issues may fester and explode into tomorrow's widespread but preventable consumer injuries," said Lee, who now leads consumer financial protection policy at nonprofit Better Markets.

Under the rules, CFPB officials select for examination companies they believe pose the highest risks to consumers, usually after months of analysis.

This year, roughly 70 companies were selected, about half the usual number, with examinations scheduled roughly evenly across four quarters, according to the people and ​a fourth person with knowledge of the matter. Reuters could ​not ascertain exactly how many firms were examined ⁠in the spring.

Examiners typically inspect records and talk with company employees to uncover any compliance or regulatory violations before deciding how to proceed. In the past, most exams moved to a "full review," involving legal analysis of violations and internal discussions on whether the issue merits enforcement action.

However, this spring examiners in most cases determined the inspections were "clean" under ​agency guidelines and proceeded with expedited reviews, the three people said. That means they determined that any violations were minor and unlikely to harm consumers, and it ​was therefore unnecessary to escalate ⁠them to legal or enforcement teams, according to public CFPB materials.

Austin Hinkle, former senior counsel in the CFPB's Supervision Division, said that expedited reviews were traditionally rare because the process was designed to focus on the riskiest companies.

"A significant number of expedited track reviews suggest to me that either political leadership simply picked the wrong companies to examine, or that when violations are identified, career staff are being told to back off," he said.

Examinations are meant in part to correct problems as ⁠they are happening. ​In the past, examiners have identified and swiftly remedied improper vehicle repossessions, harassing or abusive phone calls, attempts to collect money that borrowers do ​not owe, overcharges and unjustified fees, according to CFPB materials.

Lorelei Salas, who resigned last year as the CFPB's director of supervision after the agency halted the division's work, said she felt the CFPB leadership had demonized supervisory staff.

She added that by no longer focusing on nonbanks, it was ​ignoring "companies that pose the highest risks to consumers" at a time when many are struggling.

"The picture is pretty grim for consumers in the United States," she said.

items.title: US televangelist Jim Bakker, ensnared in fraud and sex scandal, dead at 86
items.content_html:
Oct 5 (Reuters) - U.S. televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, fraud conviction for bilking followers and divorce from television co-host Tammy Faye, died on Monday at age 86.

The death of ​Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media ‌by his second wife, Lori Bakker.

"It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening," she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband's latest television ministry.

She paid tribute to Bakker as a "pioneer of Christian television," but the cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed.

Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of ​President Donald Trump, who was known for his own brand of right-wing populism.

Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on U.S. television in the 1980s, achieving fame on ​the show "The PTL Club." PTL stood for "Praise The Lord" and "People That Love."

Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should ⁠have stood for "pass the loot."

Bakker spent 4-1/2 years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving vacations at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort.

Prosecutors painted him ​as a selfish and petty con man driven by greed and lust for power.

"Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests," Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing ​him.

Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent $265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked.

Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers ​on 200 TV stations and raked in $129 million a year.

With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk.

He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message - although it was ​larded with requests for money donations.

Tammy Faye was more much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy makeup smeared on her face.

Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on ‌all 24 fraud ⁠and conspiracy charges brought against him.

Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of $158 million by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide.

They said he siphoned $3.7 million to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants - and an air-conditioned dog house.

The judge ordered Bakker to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. "I have sinned," Bakker told the court. "I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone."

Bakker's chief aide, Richard Dortch, served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker.

Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the ​trial - even singing to reporters after his conviction - but ​divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. ⁠She died of cancer in 2007.

Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the "prosperity gospel" he once preached and writing a book titled "I Was Wrong."

"I've had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me," Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, who he married ​in 1998.

They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping "The Jim Bakker Show" at a 600-acre (240-hectare) development called Morningside near the tourism city of ​Branson, Missouri, that bore similarities ⁠to Heritage USA.

Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations.

In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for COVID-19 during the deadly coronavirus pandemic.

Bakker also said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first U.S. president to be impeached twice.

James Orson Bakker was born on January 2, 1940, the son of an auto parts factory worker in Muskegon, Michigan, who ⁠maintained a strict ​fundamentalist Christian household.

He met Tammy Faye LaValley at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis and they married in 1961. Both dropped out of ​school to become traveling evangelists as he pursued the career of a minister of the Pentecostalist Assemblies of God denomination.

Their big break came in 1964, when televangelist Pat Robertson aired a children's religious puppet show with them on his fledgling TV network.

Setting out on his own ​in the 1970s, Bakker used the emerging world of cable and satellite TV to build an empire.

items.title: Woman at center of Cornell rape allegations targeted with threats, lawyer says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 4 (Reuters) - The ​woman who has alleged she was drugged and raped by Cornell University students has been the target ‌of threats, her lawyer said on Sunday.

Thomas Giuffra, who represents the woman identified as "Jane Doe," told CNN that people have threatened to silence or harm her if she does not withdraw her civil lawsuit alleging that several members of a Cornell fraternity drugged and raped her in 2024.

"She's received ​multiple threats," Giuffra said on CNN's "State of the Union."

Giuffra said he had also been threatened.

"I'm not afraid of these ​people," he said. "But the threats, the abuse to protect what's going on, the status quo — these ⁠guys are disgusting. They should stay in their mother's basement and stay out of the world."

The identity of Jane Doe ​has become part of the fevered online conversation surrounding the case. Women on social media have been posting #IamJaneDoe in solidarity with the ​accuser and to counter some who have sought to publicly name her.

Michael Tracey, an independent journalist and commentator, posted on Friday what he said was the accuser's name, which Reuters was unable to verify, before quickly deleting it, saying his point had been made.

He has expressed sympathy for ​the accused men over what he says is the harassment they have faced, and described his effort to name the Cornell ​accuser as journalistic diligence protected under the Constitution as free speech.

He told Reuters on Sunday that he did not wish to encourage threats ‌or harassment ⁠against the woman.

"The point, from my perspective, was more about the public-policy implications of this increasingly commonly used tactic in civil litigation, for plaintiffs' attorneys to introduce sensational, reputation-harming allegations using the cloak of anonymity for their clients," Tracey said in an interview.

Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said in a video message on Saturday that the university will examine the role of fraternities and ​sororities on campus following the outcry ​over the school's handling of ⁠the rape allegations.

"At their best, these organizations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community," he said. "But being part of a group can never diminish individual ​responsibility."

Since the lawsuit was filed last month, prosecutors in Tompkins County, New York, have been ​criticized for their ⁠initial handling of the allegations in 2024. New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week named state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to look into the case.

US President Donald Trump, a critic of James for years, lambasted the decision to appoint her. "And I feel ⁠badly for ​whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake," Trump told ​reporters on Friday.

Asked about Trump's comment, Giuffra said the case shouldn't be politicized. "It has nothing to do with politics," Giuffra said.

items.title: Trump floats turning his Florida golf course into presidential retreat
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trumpon Wednesday backed a plan to turn part of his West ​Palm Beach, Florida, golf course into a Camp David-style presidential retreat.

"It's a ‌great idea, and it will be used a lot," Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked about the plan.

"The advantage is — this was suggested ​to me by the military and Secret Service — there ​are no high buildings looming over it," Trump told ⁠reporters. He also noted the location's proximity to the recently renamed President Donald ​J. Trump International Airport and a lack of nearby housing.

"They asked if I'd be ​willing to do it, and I said I would be," Trump said. "This wouldn't be for me. This would be for all future presidents."

The club was ​the site of a foiled assassination attempt on Trump in ​2024. Ryan Routh was sentenced to life in prison in February after prosecutors said ‌he ⁠hid in bushes near the course with a semi-automatic rifle. Secret Service agents captured him before he could fire a shot.

The Palm Beach Post first reported that a lawyer representing Trump International ​Golf Club proposed ​the idea in ⁠a letter last month to Palm Beach County officials. The plan would designate a parcel of the club as a permanent ​location for presidents and world leaders, the newspaper ​said. ⁠Reuters could not immediately confirm the letter's contents.

An attorney representing the club told the Washington Post that Trump would pay for construction ⁠of the ​presidential residence and facilities.

The US Secret Service and ​Department of Defense did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

(This story has refiled to remove the extraneous word 'secret' in paragraph 5.)

items.title: Michigan Republican Rogers calls for end to Canada tariff fight, breaking with Trump again
items.content_html:
Oct 7 (Reuters) - Michigan Republican Mike Rogers, locked in one of the nation's most competitive Senate races, called on Wednesday for an end to the US-Canada tariff dispute, breaking with ​President Donald Trump on a second major issue ahead of next month's election.

Rogers, who has largely backed ‌Trump's tariffs, including those on Canada, said in an ad posted on X that the trade fight with Michigan's northern neighbor should end immediately to ease costs for businesses and consumers.

"Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy," Rogers says in the ad, ​seated at a neighborhood bar with his hand wrapped around a bottle of Labatt Blue, a Canadian ​beer brand popular in Michigan, as he underscores the state's close ties to Canada. "We need ⁠to end this tariff war now.”

Rogers, who is running neck-and-neck with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in public polling, reiterated an argument ​that he could leverage his ties to Trump to resolve the dispute. "As Michigan Senator, I'll bring both parties together to ​lower your prices. That's job number one," Rogers said in the ad.

The current dispute dates to July, when Trump unveiled new tariffs on Canadian imports that took effect the following month, prompting retaliatory measures from Canada. The issue is especially sensitive in Michigan, where automakers ​depend on integrated cross-border supply chains and industry leaders have warned that a prolonged trade war could threaten jobs.

Republican ​candidates in northern border states hit hardest by the tariffs, including Rogers, have sought to balance appeals to Trump's loyal base with efforts ‌to ⁠win over independent voters, who polls show have grown increasingly critical of his handling of the economy and trade relations with Canada.

As recently as last month, Rogers had praised Trump's tariffs as part of the president's America First agenda, calling them "necessary" while cautioning that they were "not a one-size-fits-all solution."

In response, El-Sayed said Rogers' shift on tariffs reflected concern about his standing ​in the race, which the ​nonpartisan election forecaster Cook ⁠Political Report rates a "toss-up."

"You cheerled this tariff war from the beginning and you’re flip-flopping now because your poll numbers are in free fall," El-Sayed said in a statement.

The call for ​an immediate end to the tariffs came just two weeks after Rogers similarly reversed ​course on ⁠the war with Iran, which he had previously supported, urging an immediate end to the conflict as a way to lower gasoline and grocery prices.

The shifts reflect growing concerns among Republicans ahead of the November midterms, which will determine whether the ⁠party can ​hold onto its narrow House and Senate majorities. A Reuters review published on ​Wednesday found that two-thirds of Republican candidates in competitive House and Senate races have either broken with Trump on policy issues or sought to ​create some distance from him this year.

items.title: US proposes to boost transit funding to areas with higher marriage, birth rates
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - The US Transportation Department said on Wednesday it is proposing to boost grants for major transit projects ​by 10% in areas that have above-average marriage and birth rates and imposing ‌strict deadlines to ensure projects remain on schedule.

Democrats criticized the plan, which would apply to 40 major projects already in the program that funds light rail, bus and commuter rail projects and said it could ​result in lower spending in cities controlled by Democrats.

The Transportation Department awards about $20 billion ​annually in transit grants. Democrats in August criticized the agency for not awarding $1.9 ⁠billion for major transit projects.

"Tying funding for transit projects to marriage rates and how ​many babies a woman has is the sort of bizarre and dystopian idea you’d expect in ​a TV show, not actual policy put forth by the U.S. government," Democratic Senator Patty Murray said on Wednesday.

The projects that risk facing spending cuts include Washington's Red Line subway modernization program, Boston's Green Line subway ​project, an expansion of the BART train in Silicon Valley and an Austin light rail ​project, Murray said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in January 2025 signed a memo giving preference for transit grants to ‌communities ⁠with higher marriage and birth rates.

Murray cited a study showing the change would likely deprive historically underfunded urban neighborhoods of funding while benefiting higher-income areas and those with larger white populations.

The Transportation Department said the changes included setting strict deadlines and demanding local accountability on projects up ​front "so we can finally ​build these systems faster, ⁠better, and safer... If you want federal funding, your project needs to align with where communities and families are actually growing."

Murray said the ​new guidance could force "transit agencies and local and state governments that have ​already spent ⁠years planning and designing projects to follow a whole slew of new rating and cost-share requirements."

She argued it was "another attempt by the Trump administration to penalize blue states and slow down and delay ⁠transit ​projects."

In October 2025, the Transportation Department froze billions of ​dollars in funding for infrastructure projects in New York and Chicago after Trump blamed a partial government shutdown on Democrats ​in Congress, but those decisions were overturned by judges.

items.title: US agency to rewrite rules to address vehicle headlight glare
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 6 (Reuters) - The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said on Tuesday that it will rewrite its vehicle lighting ​standards to address concerns about headlight glare and allow for the latest ‌safety-improving lighting technologies.

NHTSA said it plans to improve rules for LEDs, dusk sensors, automatic high beams and replaceable light sources. The agency will also evaluate headlamp height and aim and how they ​impact driver visibility and address headlight glare and make appropriate changes.

Complaints about glare ​from headlights have increased and some lawmakers have urged the government to ⁠set a maximum headlight brightness standard. A growing number of taller trucks and ​SUVs on roads has also led to more complaints about glare.

LEDs, which now account for ​most headlights in new cars, are much brighter than traditional halogen headlights.

“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together ​to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare," said NHTSA Administrator Jonathan ​Morrison.

The issue still accounts for a small number of nighttime crashes, according to a study last year ‌from ⁠the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

The study noted that headlight glare contributes to far fewer crashes than insufficient visibility. From 2015 to 2023, headlight glare was cited as a factor in only one or two out of every 1,000 nighttime crashes across 11 ​US states, the study ​shows.

Federal headlight standards for ⁠minimum and maximum brightness have not changed since 1997, IIHS noted. The study found that drivers older than 70 appear to ​be most affected by headlight glare.

In 2022, NHTSA said it would ​allow automakers ⁠to install adaptive driving beam headlights on new vehicles. The devices adjust the headlight beam pattern to dim portions directed at other vehicles.

NHTSA will use a negotiated rulemaking process to ⁠update ​its vehicle lighting standards. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will ​appoint up to 18 people from vehicle lighting manufacturers, motor vehicle equipment associations, safety organizations, research institutions, and ​engineering associations to take part.

items.title: Conservative anti-tax group seeks FCC approval for AI robocalls ahead of US midterms
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - A Democratic member of the Federal Communications Commission urged the agency on Wednesday not to approve a ​petition to allow political AI-generated robocalls from conservative political group Club for Growth.

The group, ‌which is spending millions of dollars ahead of the November US congressional elections, asked the FCC to allow it to make political calls to cell phones "using an artificial or prerecorded voice - including an AI-generated voice - without obtaining prior ​express consent."

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez said that if "the FCC allows a dark money group ​to flood Americans' phones with AI-generated robocalls they never agreed to receive, it ⁠would bring chaos so close to Election Day."

She added that "consumers reasonably expect the rules protecting them ​from unwanted robocalls to hold steady while they decide how to vote, not for the FCC ​to change them at the 11th hour to unleash a deluge of political AI slop on their phones."

Club for Growth President David McIntosh said in a statement that the group wants "the FCC to treat First Amendment-protected political speech the ​same way it already treats wireless calls about package deliveries, bank accounts, and doctor's appointments."

The group, ​which backs conservative economic views on taxes, regulations and cutting the size of government, plans to spend $175 million in ‌the ⁠midterm congressional elections, it said on its website.

The group argued it is incorrect to refer to the calls as robocalls because a human initiates the dial to a cell phone and then an AI agent handles an interview.

The FCC, in describing the petition, said the system "uses a perfunctory human ​being for the sole ​purpose of clicking on ⁠a ‘send’ or similarly termed button to transmit thousands of text messages per hour."

A number of public interest groups on Monday urged the FCC ​not to grant the petition.

"Using robocalls, a hated form of communication, to ​deliver political messages, ⁠a sensitive topic almost nobody wants to hear about from AI-generated strangers, will enrage a wide swath of the 98% of the country that has a cellphone," said the comment signed by groups including ⁠the ​Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, Consumer Federation of ​America, Common Cause and Public Citizen.

The FCC is considering comments on the petition until October 19. A spokesman for ​FCC Chair Brendan Carr declined immediate comment.

items.title: NY Fed September survey finds public expecting more near-term inflation
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 7 (Reuters) - The public’s near-term expected path for inflation jumped ​in September to its highest level in over three years as households downgraded both their current and future ‌financial outlooks, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said on Wednesday.

Respondents to the bank’s latest Survey of Consumer Expectations said that they project inflation a year from now to hit 3.9%, the highest level since May 2023, from August’s forecast of 3.6%. Inflation three years from now is seen at 3.3% versus ​3.2% in August, while expected inflation five years from now held steady at 3%.

The deterioration in the inflation outlook came ​as households forecast future increases for all the categories the bank tracks: gas, food, rent, medical care and ⁠college costs.

The New York Fed report tracking the public’s souring mood lines up with other recent reports showing downbeat consumers in an ​economy that continues to suffer from high and persistent levels of inflation.

The report lands as pivotal midterm elections loom, with polls suggesting President ​Donald Trump and Republicans are in for a rough ride amid an ongoing affordability crisis in the US economy, which in large part is tied to their policy actions.

The main drivers of current outsized inflation gains are the ongoing impact of the president’s trade tariffs and the energy price surges caused by the ​war in the Middle East, coupled with pressure from the frenzied pace of investment in the tech sector, in the view of many ​Fed officials.

Faced with inflation that continues to outstrip the Fed’s 2% goal, officials last month raised their interest rate target by a quarter percentage point ‌to between ⁠3.75% and 4%. Officials also expect to raise rates again by year end, with investors eyeing the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting as the most likely time for action after several key officials last week said the central bank has time to weigh the data before acting again.

Minneapolis Fed leader Neel Kashkari said in an interview with Reuters last week that rough consumer confidence data is primarily a product of ​the state of price pressures.

“I still ​think it's inflation” that’s weighing ⁠on sentiment, Kashkari said. “Once we get inflation back down to 2% and people don't have to worry about it getting worse, then they can start to heal from what they've experienced over the last ​five years,” he said.

The New York Fed report found that households in September downgraded their views ​of their current and ⁠future finances, while also marking down their ability to access credit now. That said, households in September became less worried about missing a debt payment.

The September survey also found a somewhat positive arc for the public’s job market assessments. Relative to August, respondents lowered expectations the unemployment rate ⁠will be ​higher in a year. They also downgraded expectations of an involuntary job loss ​a year from now compared to August, while increasing their confidence they could find a job if they lost their current position.

The report also noted that households in September ​planned to increase future spending compared to August, for the highest reading since May 2023.

items.title: Georgia arrests man over attempted $700,000 uranium sale
items.content_html:
TBILISI, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Georgia has detained a man who planned to sell uranium-238 to a foreign national ​for $700,000, the national security service said on Wednesday.

The ‌Georgian citizen is accused of illegally handling nuclear material and faces up to 10 years in prison, it ​said in a statement, sharing a video of ​armed security personnel pulling a man out ⁠of a white sedan and handcuffing him on ​the ground.

It was not immediately possible to contact the ​man or a legal representative for comment.

The footage also showed agents testing two small containers in the trunk of ​the vehicle with a handheld radiation detector. One ​of them appeared to contain a light-coloured powder.

Uranium-238 is the most ‌common ⁠uranium isotope and, while radioactive, is not ordinarily usable on its own to make a nuclear bomb.

The security of nuclear materials was one of the ​biggest concerns ​after the ⁠1991 fall of the Soviet Union, of which Georgia was part. There have ​been several serious incidents involving the ​illicit trade ⁠in nuclear materials in Georgia over recent decades.

In February, Georgia detained two people who attempted to purchase $3 million ⁠worth ​of uranium and a cache ​of a radioactive isotope found in nuclear weapons testing programmes.

items.title: Tennessee execution survivor Christa Pike is conscious and speaking, lawyers say
items.content_html:
Oct 6 (Reuters) - Convicted killer Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee's effort to execute her by lethal injection last week, foiling the state's ​first attempt to put a woman to death in two centuries, has regained consciousness and is speaking, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday.

Despite severe injuries to her ‌arms from the insertion of intravenous lines during the aborted execution last Wednesday, Pike, 50, is "still handcuffed and shackled" to her hospital bed while she remains under medical care, her team of public defense attorneys wrote.

"Her prognosis remains unclear, but at a minimum we expect a long recovery," the lawyers' statement said, adding that a court hearing on Pike's case was scheduled for Wednesday in Davidson County Chancery Court.

The hearing pertains to her lawyers' request for a court order to preserve evidence from the ​failed execution they said would show the Tennessee Department of Correction violated Pike's constitutional rights by subjecting her to cruel and unusual punishment, a spokesperson said.

She was not expected to appear ​for the proceeding.

Pike, sentenced to death for her role as a teenager in the torture-murder of 19-year-old schoolmate Colleen Slemmer three decades ago, survived the execution attempt ⁠on the night of September 30 at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital. She has been hospitalized since then.

Her lawyers said on Friday their client remained unconscious, critically ill and hooked to ​a ventilator to breathe, as doctors labored to clear the drug pentobarbital from her system.

"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care," they wrote on Tuesday.

Pike's petition for ​clemency, denied last week by Republican Governor Bill Lee, argued her death sentence had failed to properly account for Pike's own childhood trauma as the victim of sexual abuse, neglect and untreated mental illness.

Long the only woman on death row in the state, Pike also has endured nearly 30 years of solitary confinement, her lawyers say.

Pike went from being the first woman Tennessee had tried to put to death since the early 19th century to becoming the first person in the United States ​known to have survived after execution drugs were administered.

Death penalty opponents said the incident exposed the inherent barbarity of executions. It also highlighted the difficulties of carrying out lethal injections while respecting constitutional prohibitions on ​cruel and unusual punishment.

Pike's attorneys and journalists who witnessed the execution attempt described it as roughly 2-1/2 hours of disarray and prolonged distress for her as Correction Department personnel struggled to administer two doses of pentobarbital intravenously.

Pike ‌was heard gasping, ⁠crying, whimpering and breathing loudly through much of the procedure, at one point saying, "My arm feels like it's about to burst open."

The bungled attempt to establish intravenous lines left both of Pike's arms "swollen, burned and blistered," the apparent result of the pentobarbital, a highly alkaline and caustic substance, seeping into the tissues under her skin, her lawyers said in court filings.

The lawyers accused state officials of having shrugged off prior warnings from Pike's doctors that her small veins and a blood disorder would make placing IV lines especially difficult.

In the midst of the procedure, Pike's lawyers filed an emergency court motion to halt it. By then, prison ​officials had ceased their execution efforts and called an ​ambulance, according to court records.

The night of ⁠the execution attempt, the Correction Department defended its handling of the situation, saying it had "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol." But agency commissioner Frank Strada has resigned and will leave his post this month, the governor announced on Saturday.

Lee had previously ordered a suspension of any scheduled executions for the rest of ​the year and a third-party review of what happened in Pike's case.

Two days before Pike was due to meet her fate, Lee rejected a ​petition seeking to commute her ⁠death penalty to a life prison term without the possibility of parole.

Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, and a third companion lured Slemmer into a wooded area on the University of Tennessee campus in Knoxville and killed her.

The gruesome nature of the slaying, which involved Shipp carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and Pike bashing Slemmer in the head with a chunk of asphalt, ⁠then taking a ​piece of her skull as a souvenir, drew intense media coverage at the time. Trial testimony indicated Pike viewed Slemmer as ​a rival for her boyfriend's affections.

Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the ​time of the murder and had acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.

items.title: US FAA says Boeing 737 MAX software glitch poses no safety issue
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 2 (Reuters) - The Federal Aviation Administration said on Friday that a panel of experts had determined a software ‌glitch in some Boeing 737 MAX flight computers poses no safety concern, clearing the way for approval of the best-selling narrow-body jet's largest variant.

The decision removes a late obstacle to certification of the 737 MAX 10, which has been delayed for years. It should also ease concerns at airlines that fly the MAX 7, ​which uses the same software and was certified by the FAA in August.

The FAA said the determination by the Corrective ​Action Review Board that met in Seattle on Friday was based on the fact that "pilots retain full ⁠control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous."

This week, the FAA said it was delaying ​certification of the MAX 10 until it completed an analysis of the software issue, which could prevent pilots from accessing automated flight guidance ​during an unusual landing scenario.

Senior officials at the US regulator were alerted to it in August, nearly two years after Canadian carrier WestJet first flagged the issue to Boeing.

WestJet discovered the anomaly during an entry-into-service test flight, the airline said on Friday in a staff memo seen by Reuters. It ​said the vertical navigation mode, which automates a plane’s vertical flight path, disengaged during approach.

WestJet, which expects to take the MAX ​10 early next year, uses the affected software, U14.1, on its MAX jets.

“WestJet has received no reports of this condition occurring during normal line operations,” ‌the memo ⁠said. “Very few occurrences have been reported by other operators using U14 or U14.1 because the condition requires a specific sequence of events.”

Boeing said it "will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our engineers work on the next software update." Boeing added it was working with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots "to re-enable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur."

The FAA had said ​the latest software version can ​increase pilot workload during a ⁠go-around, a situation in which a pilot aborts a landing attempt, applies power, and climbs to make another landing attempt.

Major US airlines had opted to use an earlier version of the software while ​the analysis was underway.

Aviation officials now believe the MAX 10 could be certified as soon as ​later this month, in line ⁠with earlier expectations. The issue could also have affected Southwest Airlines (LUV.N), opens new tab because the same software is used on the newly certified MAX 7 airplane.

Other large airlines, including Alaska Airlines (ALK.N), opens new tab and United Airlines (UAL.O), opens new tab, that have ordered the MAX 10 could also have been impacted by a lengthy delay.

Jefferies ⁠said in ​a research note the decision allows the MAX 10 to be certified before the ​end of the year and estimated Boeing has nearly 1,500 MAX 10s on order from airlines.

An FAA official said it would issue a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin to US airlines ​and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin.

items.title: 'I'm getting fed up': early US midterm voters line up before dawn in Ohio
items.content_html:
MEDINA, Ohio, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Voters started lining up while it was still dark on Tuesday morning at the Medina County Board of Elections as early voting began in Ohio, a state that looms large in the nationwide campaigns between Republicans and Democrats battling for ​control of the US Congress.

By the time polling in the northeast Ohio county closed for the day, Democrats' turnout eclipsed that of Republicans' in a possible early sign that they are more motivated to vote this year.

Though turnout ‌is typically higher in presidential elections, which are run every four years, this year's midterm voters in Ohio have a say in one key US Senate race and two for the US House of Representatives that are seen as "toss-ups," according to the Cook Political Report.

Registered Republicans, Democrats and independents interviewed by Reuters all shared similar frustrations: they are exhausted by political ads they see as deceptive and mean, they hate the US war with Iran and they really hate the inflation that they believe has become chronic.

Nobody said they expected things to improved any time soon.

The third person in line waiting for polling to open at 8 a.m. (1200 GMT) ​was Eddie St. John, 83, a retiree from the town of Wadsworth. Asked what he most wanted to see fixed as a result of the election, which ends on November 3, St. John said, "Mostly it's our economy. It sucks."

"You can't ​afford nothing anymore. Everything's so high. Gas is getting worse all the time," he said, adding, "This guy in office now he promises this. He promises that... (but) nothing's coming down."

"This guy," St. John said, ⁠is President Donald Trump, who isn't on the ballot but whom the voter said he blames more than political parties.

The party in power usually suffers in midterm elections. With Republicans holding the White House and both chambers of Congress at a time when ​Trump's approval rating is at a record-low 32%, Democrats are feeling increasingly competitive.

Political analysts will be watching closely what unfolds in Ohio, as Trump has been a dominant force, especially among blue-collar workers who used to align with the Democratic Party.

But with inflation running at around ​3.4%, there is deep discontent over rising food, energy and housing costs.

The US war with Iran, launched by Trump on February 28 for reasons that critics say he has not clearly articulated, also has voters worried that it will become yet another "forever war."

Troy Flohr, 59, a retired policeman with the Medina County Sheriff, complained about the array of campaign ads that he said were riddled with "half-truths."

Standing just feet away from a voting booth, Flohr said he usually backs Republicans but was still undecided whether to vote to reelect Republican Representative Max Miller for a third term. "I tend to like the rest of them" running as Republicans on this year's ​ballot, Flohr added.

He said his nephew is serving in the US Army and stationed in the Middle East.

Without mentioning Trump by name, he said, "I'm tired of him saying the war's going to end in two weeks, the war's going to end next month...I'm getting fed ​up with that."

Yet Flohr said he would "probably" vote for Trump again given the chance. "I don't like where the Democrat Party has gone. I'm going to leave the rest of that comment alone," he said when asked to elaborate.

Trump won Ohio and the state's 17 electoral votes handily in ‌2016, 2020 and 2024, ⁠despite losing the 2020 presidential race to Democrat Joe Biden.

This election could depend on whether disaffected Democrats return to their party and whether many independents turn their backs on Trump's Republicans.

Medina County, seen as a swing district, has 132,345 registered voters of which 29,466 are Republicans and 15,872 Democrats. Election officials say there are 86,762 independents, who could determine whether Republicans continue their success there.

Despite Republicans' advantage in registered voters in the county, 499 Democrats cast ballots on Tuesday, compared to 374 Republicans, along with 291 independents. That is a significant reversal from the first day of voting in 2024, when 369 Democrats voted, compared to 702 Republicans and 433 independents, according to county data.
