Even more telling is data from the 2022 midterm election, when 198 Republicans cast a vote in the first day of early voting, ​compared to 139 Democrats and 68 independents.

Former Senator ​Sherrod Brown, a Democrat from Ohio, is trying to return ⁠to the Senate, where he served for 18 years before being defeated two years ago by Republican Senator Bernie Moreno.

This time around, Brown, a populist Democrat who long railed against US trade deals with foreign competitors, is attempting to unseat Republican Jon Husted in a special election with the winner holding the seat through 2028.

Political analysts see the race between Husted and Brown as a toss-up.

With Republicans currently holding ​a 53-47 majority in the Senate, Democrats are hoping for a net gain of at least four seats, including in Ohio, in order to control the chamber.

Meanwhile, two neck-and-neck ​US House races could help determine next ⁠year's majority in that chamber, which Republicans currently hold with a 218-214 margin. One independent is aligned with Republicans and there are two vacancies that will be filled in the midterm elections.

In the 7th congressional district, which includes Medina, just south of Cleveland, incumbent Miller is seen facing a tough challenge from Democrat Brian Poindexter.

While Miller has raised far more funds than his Democratic opponent and has Trump's endorsement in a Republican-leaning district, his campaign has been hit by allegations of domestic violence, which he denies.

Poindexter is a labor union ironworker and member of a suburban ⁠city council.

Meanwhile, in ​Ohio's 9th congressional district that covers most of northwest Ohio and hugs the shores of Lake Erie, Democratic Representative Marcy Kaptur, a moderate who was first elected ​in 1982, is battling in another toss-up race against Republican challenger Derek Merrin, who nearly defeated her in 2024.

Annie Wild, 64, a retired public school teacher, said she will vote for all Democrats on the ballot. She also said since the early days of Trump's second term she has begun to see some of the president's ​supporters saying they are abandoning him. But that is not coming from the voters she called "MAGA."

"I've lost friends that I've had for 50 years," she said of some Trump supporters, because of the gulf between them.

items.title: US Senator Murphy says Pentagon denied him access to US base in Qatar
items.content_html:
RIYADH, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy said on Tuesday that the Department of Defense denied him access to ​a key military base in Qatar during a visit to the Middle East, describing ‌it as part of a US government effort to conceal the impact of the Iran war.

The Al Udeid Air Base is the largest US base in the region and has repeatedly been attacked by Iran ​during the war launched by the US and Israel in February.

"This trip confirmed for ​me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide ⁠the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and ​the American people," Murphy told a group of journalists in Riyadh, the second stop on ​his trip.

Many members of Congress, including some of President Donald Trump's Republicans, have been pushing his administration to provide them with more information about the cost of the war, strategy and casualties.

Asked for comment, ​a senior Pentagon official said Murphy's office had been informed before his trip that ​he would not receive the department's support to access the base, consistent with Secretary of Defense Pete ‌Hegseth's ⁠March 3, 2026, directive restricting travel to the area.

"The Department applies the Secretary's guidance evenly," the official said in an emailed statement.

Murphy said that the Pentagon refused to set up a briefing for him on the war while he was in the region.

"I've never encountered ​anything like this in ​my time in ⁠the Senate and it's part of a deliberate campaign of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an end to," ​he said.

He said that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had ​facilitated his ⁠visit, including arranging meetings with diplomats, a stance he contrasted with that of the Pentagon.

During his trip, Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee who represents the state of Connecticut, ⁠met ​with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani ​and with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as well as other senior Gulf officials.

items.title: Trump orders firing squad for gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 6 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad to execute the former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree the gunman later described as retaliation for US wars in the Muslim world, the Pentagon said.

Putting former US Army Major Nidal Hasan to death by Army firing ​squad was approved by Trump at the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X on Monday.

Parnell ​noted that Hasan shouted "Allahu Akbar" — God is greatest in Arabic — during the attack, which killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and ⁠a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others.

Acting US Army Secretary Adam Telle said on X on Tuesday that the execution by firing squad will ​take place on December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas.

Death by firing squad was one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to ​permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation.

The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times.

Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman ​for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched an attempt to administer a lethal injection, leaving the ​death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalized.

Her lawyers said on Tuesday she regained consciousness. "Her prognosis remains unclear, but at a minimum we expect a long recovery," the lawyers ‌said on ⁠Tuesday.

Pike's lawyers had previously urged the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection, such as hanging or firing squad, in anticipation of the trouble executioners faced in establishing a sound intravenous line.

A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military ​base.

The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now ​56, was scheduled to be ⁠deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.

In a statement responding to Trump's decision, the group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said: "There is nothing ​Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill."

Military executions are rare, and under the Uniform Code of ​Military Justice, a death ⁠sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out "until approved by the president."

If Hasan is put to death, it would mark the first military execution since 1961, the group said. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US ⁠military firing ​squad was one carried out "by musketry" in November 1945, the center reported.

At least five states ​have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

items.title: US Coast Guard finds debris from missing medical aircraft off Nantucket
items.content_html:
Oct 3 (Reuters) - The US Coast Guard said late on Saturday it ​found debris from a medical transport aircraft off the shore of ‌Massachusetts' Nantucket island and was searching for six people who were on board.

The Federal Aviation Administration told the Coast Guard early on Saturday that it had lost contact with a Gulfstream jet ​traveling from Bermuda to Boston. Several hours later, the Coast Guard said in ​a statement that it "located a debris field that has been confirmed ⁠to be associated with the missing aircraft."

Four Canadians were on the plane, Canadian ​Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X.

"We are closely monitoring the situation and ​are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue," he wrote.

The other two passengers were Bermudian nationals, the Coast Guard said. Searches will continue throughout the night near Nantucket, an ​island community south of mainland Massachusetts, they said.

The aircraft, registered to Latitude Air ​Ambulance, departed Bermuda at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday (0301 GMT), according to data from flight tracking website FlightAware. ‌The plane ⁠was flying at 24,000 feet (7,300 metres) for much of the flight before descending 13,000 feet in about two minutes shortly before flight controllers lost contact, data showed.

Local TV station Boston 25 posted an audio clip from Boston Logan International Airport in which ​an air traffic ​controller can be heard ⁠asking the Gulfstream pilot, "You said you're coming in blind? Is that what you said?"

The controller then asked whether the plane was ​declaring an emergency. No response was heard.

Latitude is based in ​Ontario, Canada, ⁠and provides medical evacuation services. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and the families of the passengers, Bermuda ⁠Premier David ​Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram.

"We ​are praying that all six people will be found safe," he wrote.

items.title: Transcript of US Vice President Vance interview in Alaska
items.content_html:
FAIRBANKS, Alaska, Oct 6 (Reuters) - US Vice President JD Vance gave an exclusive interview to Reuters on Monday while campaigning in Alaska, a state that has emerged as a key battleground in the November elections that will determine control of Congress.

This transcript of the interview, which took place after a rally at Fairbanks International Airport for Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan, has been edited lightly for length and clarity.

Jacob Bogage, Reuters:

Mr. Vice President, let's start here. Can you tell me about where things stand ​with Iran right now?

Vice President JD Vance:

Well, you know, we're at a place where the Iranians are trying to terrorize the world economy by shooting at commercial shipping. They're largely failing. They're hitting some ships, but not enough to stop the flow of oil and gas. So what that means is, their response ‌to us destroying the nuclear program was to try to terrorize commercial shipping and exercise leverage over the United States of America.

And where we are is, as the president said, the nuclear program's been destroyed, but every time they try to squeeze the world economy, we actually squeeze them harder. And so I think what the president has said is, look, you guys fundamentally are not in a game that's going to work out for you. Every time they try to cause damage to the world economy, they end up causing much greater damage to themselves, and eventually they're going to have to decide either to make smarter decisions or to suffer the consequences.

Bogage:

You've played a pivotal role in terms of American foreign policy writ large, turning how the US engages on the world's stage from conflicts without direct American interests, like Ukraine, to conflicts with direct American interests, like Iran. Tell me ​a little bit about what does it take for the US to resume kinetic attacks? What do you need to hear? Or, rather, what do you need to not hear?

Vance:

That's obviously a decision the president of the United States will make. But you know, we have to start with a fundamental goal here. The goal here is to prevent ​the Iranians from having a nuclear weapon, and really to prevent regional nuclear proliferation. Because, as the president's reminded people, it's if the Iranians get a nuclear weapon, then other countries will get a nuclear weapon.

Bogage:

Is that a larger focus than where this conflict began?

Vance:

To finish that ⁠question, what that means is their nuclear facilities, their enrichment facilities, have been destroyed, and we're going to ensure that they can't rebuild those facilities and rebuild their nuclear capacity.

That's fundamentally the goal here, and everything else that's happening, from them terrorizing shipping to our response to that, is really a subplot of the much bigger goal of keeping them from having a nuclear weapon.

Bogage:

You ​talk about preventing regional proliferation. Is that a goal that has expanded from the original goal of this operation?

Vance:

No, no. I mean, I think that's one of the reasons why the president didn't want Iran to get a nuclear weapon, because he realized that if they did, then a lot of other countries would then sprint for a nuclear weapon.

So, you know, you don't want the ​world's largest state sponsor of terrorism to have a nuclear weapon. You also don't want to radically increase the number of nuclear weapons in the world. The president hears a lot about that.

It's interesting. It's something that came up in the conversation with (Chinese President) Xi (Jinping) that the president has said multiple times publicly. He doesn't like mass proliferation of nuclear weapons. It's one of the core parts of his foreign policy, and frankly, something that both Democrats and Republicans should have been a little more focused on over the last 40 years.

Bogage:

Who is the US negotiating with right now?

Vance:

Well, that's a good question.

You know we're negotiating with the political leadership of the country, specifically, you know, the foreign minister has led the negotiations, the president of the country, a number of people work for them. But one of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how ​their country makes decisions.

If you go back to the original agreement that we struck, it was very simple. It was not a complicated document. It basically said we're going to open up the Strait of Hormuz, the United States is going to lift our blockade, and we're going to talk about the nuclear program. That's really all it said.

And they couldn't even keep the end ​of the bargain where they didn't shoot at commercial shipping. And our assessment of why that is, is because, yeah, you have people in the country who want to make a deal, and we're willing to talk to them. You also have people in the country who are trying to sabotage a deal, which I think is very stupid for their country. But you know, it's ultimately their decision to ‌make.

Bogage:

Iran has said for ⁠47 years, and I'm not going to weigh in on whether it's believable or not, that they don't want a nuclear weapon. How do they communicate that any differently, in a way that helps the United States wind down its operation?

Vance:

Well, I guess I would say, if you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue.

Sixty percent enriched uranium, you know, I'm hardly a nuclear scientist, but I've learned this: you don't need that for any energy production. You don't need it for anything except to have threshold weapons-grade uranium.

So I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity. So far, we haven't seen a long-term commitment to do that.

Bogage:

There's been reporting that you are leading these talks. Are you leading these talks?

Vance:

We're certainly involved. I mean, ultimately, the president of the United States is driving things and is issuing direction. And then, you know, we're trying to get the president's mission accomplished as best we can.

You ​know, what the president has said is, you know, look, from the very beginning, we're willing ​to strike an agreement where the Iranians commit to not rebuilding their nuclear program ⁠and take real steps in order to do that, but it takes two to tango, and we're not going to trade words for actions.

In other words, the United States is not going to do things for mere promise of actions on the Iranian side. We need to trade actions for actions here, and we'll see what the Iranians do.

Bogage:

Since we spoke earlier this morning, the New York Times reported there was an Iranian operation in motion in the UK at RAF Fairford, similar to perhaps what the Ukrainians had done in getting drones deep into the country. Do you ​have any intelligence on that that you're in a position to share?

Vance:

I'm not going to speak to classified intelligence. Nothing has happened yet. We're very aware that the Iranians are trying to conduct strikes against American assets all over the world. You know, we also ​have incredibly capable guys on the military side and the ⁠intelligence side. So far, nothing has happened. We'll keep praying and working to ensure that it doesn't.

Bogage:

On munitions stocks, we hear one thing from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. We hear other things from commanders in the field, but I know you speak to them personally. Have they conveyed concern about munition stocks to you?

Vance:

I'd be surprised if the commanders in the field were saying something different than what Secretary Hegseth is saying, because obviously they're communicating to him and they're communicating to all of us.

I think what is undoubtedly true is that warfare has changed. I mean, you mentioned this Ukrainian attack on a Russian airfield, and you know whatever the reality is, people are using drones and asymmetric capabilities in a totally new way, and that does require a totally new kind of defensive and offensive capability.

Do I think ⁠that we're far ahead of ​anybody else in the world? Yeah. Do I think that we always need to be thinking about how to build more? The president, I wouldn't even say laser-focused. I would say he is obsessed with this question of ​how we stay ahead in terms of military-grade technology.

I think that sometimes this munitions conversation gets reinterpreted through a lens of American weakness, when in reality, what the president is just trying to say is, we need to build the weapons of the future, and we need to build enough so that we can properly defend ourselves.

Bogage:

It would be malpractice, Mr. Vice President, if I didn't ask this.

Vance:

Go ahead.

Bogage:

These good people at the rally seem like they want you to run ​for president. Are you going to run for president, sir?

Vance:

Man, I've been asked that question a lot. I'm inherently a procrastinator, and I really haven't thought that much about it. We're going to try to win the midterms, get Dan Sullivan elected, which I'm very confident we're going to do, and then, you know, we'll figure it out after that.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump approval falls to record low of 32% as high costs bite, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Sept 21 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's approval rating fell to ​32% - the lowest of his political career - as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran ‌war, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The poll, completed on Sunday, was conducted over a four-day period that saw Trump throw three major news organizations out of the White House and muse that Washington's iconic Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts -- named after slain President John F. Kennedy -- could be torn down if Trump's own name could not be added to it.

It found voters leaning away from supporting Trump's fellow Republicans in the ​November 3 midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.

Trump's overall approval was down from a reading of 35% in last week's ​Reuters/Ipsos poll, with support among his own Republicans down to 73% from 82% a week earlier.

Trump returned to the White House in January ⁠2025 on promises to tame inflation and end foreign wars. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the hours after he was sworn in, he enjoyed a 47% approval rating.

Just ​17% of respondents in the new poll approved of his handling of the cost of living - the top issue Americans say will determine how they vote in November.

Dissatisfaction among Republicans on inflation has been growing since Trump launched the war on Iran in February that has pushed gasoline and diesel prices sharply higher. Now for the first time, Republicans who disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living outnumber those who give him a thumbs up - 51% to 44%.

Trump's approval rating is lower than any recorded for his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, whose presidency ​was also marked by surging inflation and who ultimately ended his reelection bid after a poor debate performance heightened concerns about his age. Biden's low was 35%, reached in ​late October 2024.

Only 34% of the most recent poll respondents approve of the strikes on Iran. The conflict has cut the world off from a significant slice of the oil and gas produced ‌in the ⁠Middle East, and threatens to stoke higher inflation in the US and elsewhere as businesses pass on higher fuel costs to consumers.

Trump initially said the conflict would last a few weeks and that Iran needed to be bombed to stop it from developing nuclear weapons. Earlier this month, the Republican leader pledged the war would end "immediately after" the election. But Iran has shown no sign of giving up and in recent weeks Tehran and its allies have threatened further disruptions to oil markets.

Some 82% of poll respondents - including nine in ​ten Democrats and three-quarters of Republicans - said the ​conflict would likely go on for ⁠an "extended period of time."

The Reuters/Ipsos poll showed registered voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans - 43% to 35% - when asked how they would vote in the midterms. The 8-point gap was the biggest leadfor Democrats in Reuters/Ipsos polling this year. For Republicans, losing control of ​either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his term.

The poll results on congressional voting plans provide ​an overall view of ⁠which party Americans nationwide want to see in charge in Congress, though the results don't capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House of Representatives.

Trump remains popular among Republicans on the issue of immigration - with 79% of his party backing him - but only 36% of Americans overall support his approach to the matter ⁠and 55% disapprove. ​Some Republican allies in Congress have warned that his aggressive campaign to deport people in the country ​illegally risks alienating voters with family who recently immigrated to America, like some Hispanics.

Some 35% of poll respondents approve of Trump's approach to fighting crime, compared to 50% who disapprove.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online and gathered ​1,277 responses from US adults nationwide. It had a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

items.title: US FCC chair says government ads featuring Trump do not raise concerns
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - The chair of the US Federal Communications Commission said on Wednesday that taxpayer-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump ​are not improper and do not raise any red flags.

Democratic lawmakers ‌said the White House transferred $20 million in Homeland Security Department funds to air the ads, including one that closely resembles a 2024 Trump campaign ad.

"There's nothing in there that strikes ​me to merit any sort of FCC review or any liability for ​any broadcaster for running a regular, normal (public service announcement)," said FCC Chair Brendan ⁠Carr, a Republican who was named head of the agency by Trump in ​January 2025.

Ethics experts and lawmakers from both parties have criticized the three nationally ​broadcast ads, which celebrate a "golden age of America" and are airing five weeks before midterm elections.

Trump defended the ads on Wednesday. "I'm not running for office," he said. "If somebody said that that's wrong, ​I'll gladly pay the money. But, but these are ads for the country. ... ​I'm not promoting a candidate. I'm not promoting myself because I'm not running for office."

Lawmakers have ‌questioned ⁠whether public funds are being used to promote Trump politically, while other critics say the spots may violate longstanding restrictions on government propaganda and political activity.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, a Democrat, criticized the ads. "This administration has launched an aggressive effort ​to influence the outcome ​of the midterm ⁠elections," Gomez said.

Public Citizen filed a complaint with the FCC arguing the spots are campaign advertisements that should not be ​produced or distributed with taxpayer resources.

One ad features Trump declaring ​that "America will ⁠never be a communist country" while a chorus repeats the words "love me." Another combines images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a "golden age of America."

A ⁠third ​describes a "final battle" against the "deep state" and closely ​resembles one of Trump's 2024 campaign advertisements.

The ads end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for ​by the US government.

items.title: Trump urges supporters to vote by mail despite fraud claims
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 5 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump encouraged supporters on Saturday and again on Monday to vote by mail if they wanted, a change of tone ​for the US president, who has for years described mail-in voting ‌as a practice rife with fraud.

Speaking to reporters at the White House before departing for a rally in Nebraska on Monday afternoon, Trump said his supporters could vote by mail ​in the coming congressional midterm elections on November 3, even as he ​said he preferred in-person voting.

"They can vote by mail if ⁠they want, because we seem to have no choice because a lot of ​people want to vote by mail, but a lot of very good people ​also want to vote in-person," Trump said. "You can do either."

The comments came after he posted a campaign video over the weekend encouraging Republicans to vote.

"Vote early, vote by mail or vote in-person ​on Election Day, November 3rd," Trump said.

It was not immediately clear why ​Trump changed his tone. The president has repeatedly made false claims that his 2020 election defeat ‌was the ⁠result of voter fraud, including with mail-in ballots. The Trump administration tried to significantly tighten the rules governing mail-in voting heading into the midterm elections, though the Supreme Court in September declined to allow the Postal Service to enforce ​the new rules.

Some Republicans ​have in the ⁠past expressed concern that discouraging mail-in voting could reduce turnout among conservative rural voters, a core part of Trump's base, ​some of whom live relatively far from polling stations.

Republicans are ​entering the ⁠final weeks of the campaign in a difficult national political environment. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday found Trump's approval rating at 32%, holding at September's record low, while ⁠registered ​voters preferred Democrats over Republicans 44% to 37% ​when asked which party they would support in the midterms. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, ​with 28% undecided.

items.title: US Senator Warren presses federal housing director to cooperate with probe
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Democratic US Senator Elizabeth Warren on Tuesday pressed Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, an ally of President Donald Trump, to cooperate with a congressional ​watchdog's inquiry into his criminal referrals of alleged mortgage fraud.

In a letter sent to ‌Pulte and seen by Reuters, Warren said she believes the FHFA is obstructing inquiries from the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan government agency.

Critics say Pulte has politicized the historically low-profile FHFA since he took the helm ​in March 2025, including publicly referring to the Department of Justice allegations of mortgage ​fraud by several of Trump's perceived foes. Those accused have denied the allegations.

A ⁠spokesperson for the FHFA, which was created in response to the 2008 housing crisis to ​oversee mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, said in a statement that the agency always ​engages with GAO inquiries.

"The Agency has responded to every one of GAO's inquiries received this past fiscal year," the spokesperson said.

Pulte has previously defended the referrals as part of his efforts to root out misconduct and fraud ​in mortgage markets.

"GAO is working with the agency and Congress to obtain the information we ​need to conduct our work," a spokesperson said in a statement, declining to say more about the ongoing ‌efforts.

Last year, ⁠Warren of Massachusetts and several other Democratic senators pressed the GAO to investigate Pulte's conduct, concerned that the referrals were politically motivated and misused government resources.
